Socrates tried by 'the Athenian democracy'; Plato's Academy in Athens (Aristotle entry). Both verbatim.
469 is Socrates' birth year ('in his lifetime (469–399 B.C.E.)'), used as the school's start. Fine for a school named after two men, but it reads as 'philosophy began in 469'.
fix: Label it as lifetimes, e.g. 'WHEN: 469–347 BCE (lives of Socrates and Plato)', or use 'late 5th–mid 4th century BCE'; same two quotes support either.

note: Plato entry: 'Plato (429?–347 B.C.E.)'. Death of the second of the two named men is a fair end for this school-as-two-people.
SEP Aristotle: 'In Athens, Aristotle set up his own school ... the Lyceum'.
'before returning to Athens for the second and final time, in 335. In Athens, Aristotle set up his own school' - founding of the Lyceum.

322 is Aristotle's death (intro '384–322'); he had already left Athens in 323. The school is 'Aristotle and the Peripatetics', and the page says 'Those affiliated with Aristotle's school later came to be called Peripatetics' - the school outlived him. MISLEADING: one man's tenure stands in for a whole school.
fix: 'WHEN: from 335 BCE (Lyceum founded)' and, if an end is wanted, say 'Aristotle taught there until 323 BCE' (same section: 'After thirteen years in Athens, Aristotle once again found cause to retire from the city, in 323'). An end date for the Peripatetic school needs another source.

note: SEP Epicurus: 'In Athens, he purchased the property that became known as the “Garden” (later used as a name for his school itself)'.
SEP Philodemus: 'moved to Italy, probably in the 70s BCE ... may have lived in the Greek town of Naples'; Epicurus entry adds the Herculaneum library and Lucretius.
'returning again to Athens in 307/06 ... purchased the property ... and began to develop his own school in earnest'.

c. 30 BCE is Philodemus' death date ('ca. 110–ca. 30 BCE'). Nothing in the sources says the school ended then. MISLEADING: one man's death closes a tradition; a newcomer will read 'Epicureanism ended in 30 BCE'.
fix: 'WHEN: 307/6 BCE onward (still active in the 1st century BCE with Philodemus and Lucretius)'. Epicurus entry: 'More or less contemporary with Philodemus is Lucretius (first century B.C.E.)'. A real end date needs another source.

note: Intro: name from 'the porch (stoa poikilê) in the Agora at Athens ... where the first generation of Stoic philosophers congregated and lectured'.

Rome is right per the page, but the cited quote is about Cicero, whom the same sentence calls 'never identifying as a Stoic himself', and 'popularize it at Rome' means philosophy in general. (Quote verbatim; the page has a space before the comma after 'Cicero'.)
fix: Cite 'Stoicism became particularly fashionable in the Roman period', or 'Epictetus, a former slave, was expelled from Rome by Domitian along with other philosophers in 93 CE' (same section).

note: 'The Stoic school was founded around 300 BCE by Zeno of Citium'.

180 CE is the end of Marcus Aurelius' reign. The very next sentences name Hierocles, also 2nd century CE, and 'this remarkable span of time during which the Stoic school operated'; the intro says it 'enjoyed continued popularity in the Roman period and beyond'. MISLEADING: one emperor's reign ends a school.
fix: 'WHEN: c. 300 BCE–2nd century CE' (Hierocles: 'Also active in the second century CE'), or 'c. 300 BCE–Roman imperial era'.

note: The Academy was in Athens: 'In Athens, and as head of the Academy, he [Philo] stays relatively close to Carneades'. Arcesilaus and Carneades worked there too.

The only Rome quote is about Philo of Larissa moving to Rome, where 'he develops a markedly different position'; the page says just before it that 'With Philo, the skeptical era of Plato's Academy comes to an end'. So the quote ties Rome to the end of skepticism, not to its growth. No cited text puts the Pyrrhonists in Rome.
fix: Replace with 'Greece (Athens, Elis)': the same page names 'Pyrrho of Elis'. Or keep only 'Athens'.

note: Intro: 'The Academic and Pyrrhonian skeptical movements begin roughly in the third century BCE'.
Same sentence: 'and end with Sextus Empiricus in the second century CE'.

Egypt is right, but the quotes are Plotinus' birthplace ('Egyptian-born') and where he studied before founding the school ('moved from Alexandria to Rome'). The page does name Alexandria as a later centre, but that line isn't cited.
fix: Cite 'Hellenic philosophy and the teaching of its attendant disciplines went on in Alexandria and Constantinople until the end of the 6th century' (same section).

note: 'Plotinus moved from Alexandria to Rome and founded a school of philosophy there'.
'The most vigorous group of Neoplatonists, living in Athens' (Athens shown as the country).

SEP Origen: 'a native of Alexandria'; he worked there until 216. Note: the same section says he then 'took up residence' in Caesarea (Palestine) and finished major works there; that centre is missing from the list.
The cited quote is only Augustine's birthplace ('born in Thagaste ... modern Souk Ahras in Algeria'). The country is right for his work too, but that isn't in the cited text.
fix: Cite the same section: 'ordained a priest in the diocese of the maritime city of Hippo Regius (modern Annaba/Bône in Algeria). About five years later (ca. 396) he succeeded the local bishop'.

note: Augustine in Milan ('In 383 he moved to Milan'; baptised there) and Boethius' family in Rome ('keep up their traditions in Rome'). Both quotes are loose but true for Italy.
c. 185 is Origen's birth year ('Origen (c. 185–c. 253)'), not when anything started. No cited quote dates the start of Christian philosophy.
fix: 'WHEN: 3rd–6th century CE (Origen to Boethius)'; Origen was active in Alexandria until he 'left Alexandria in 216'. An earlier start needs another source.

note: 526 is Boethius' death ('died: 526? C.E.'). The Boethius entry calls him an intermediary 'between ancient philosophy and the Latin Middle Ages', not the end of a patristic school. So the span runs from one man's birth to another's death.
fix: As above: '3rd–6th century CE', or '... to Boethius (d. 526)' so it reads as a person, not the end of a tradition.

note: SEP medieval: 'Paris became the centre of philosophy in Latin Europe in the twelfth century'. Paris for France is fair here.
'at much the same time a university developed at Oxford'.
Twelfth-century Parisian schools ('Paris became the centre ... in the twelfth century').

The quote is about when *medieval philosophy* ended and is hedged ('Many different answers might be given ... a plausible (and to many people surprising) one is: around about 1700'). The same section has better support: university philosophy carried on until the late 17th century, and Iberian 'baroque scholasticism' in the 16th–17th. MISLEADING by omission: the late phase that justifies c. 1700 was centred in Spain, which isn't listed.
fix: Cite 'University philosophy continued in its established patterns ... until late in the seventeenth century', and add 'Spain' to places from 'In the Iberian peninsula, the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries were the period in which philosophical theology, studied in the established university manner, flourished (see entry on the School of Salamanca)'.

France is right, but the cited quote (IEP Renaissance Skepticism) is about Charron's book, judged by a later scholar as the most influential 'in French philosophy during the first half of the seventeenth century'. That is the very end of the period and about one book's later influence.
fix: Cite IEP Renaissance Skepticism: 'Academic skepticism had a major impact in mid-sixteenth century France through the pedagogical reforms proposed by Petrus Ramus (1515-1572)', or the Montaigne section.
